extracted.intended_audience: citizens and policymakers evaluating the proposed federal Constitution (delegates and voters in state ratifying conventions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and evaluative criteria for choosing the term length, apportionment rules, and size of the House of Representatives under the proposed federal Constitution. Covers safety and utility of election frequency, counting inhabitants (including slaves), representation-by-wealth considerations, and appropriate chamber size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of power to duration
rubrics_metrics.description: Where no other circumstances affect the case, 'the greater the power is, the shorter ought to be its duration; and, conversely, the smaller the power, the more safely may its duration be protracted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the scope of legislative power as a guide to appropriate term length: bodies with greater authority require more frequent accountability; less powerful bodies may safely have longer terms. Madison uses this as a general maxim to compare the federal legislature to the British Parliament and colonial assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election frequency — safety of biennial elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Biennial elections will be as safe to the liberty of the people as more frequent elections, particularly when fixed by a paramount Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments supporting biennial (two-year) terms: (1) the federal legislature will possess only part of supreme legislative authority (less danger); (2) it will be watched and controlled by state legislatures (additional checks); (3) the more permanent branches of the federal government will have less effective means to seduce the House. Contrast with Britain, where without a superior constitution Parliament could change its own term and even extend itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election frequency — usefulness/competence of longer terms
rubrics_metrics.description: A period of service should bear proportion to the practical knowledge required; two years is more appropriate for federal legislators than one year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal representatives need experience and information not only about local laws but the diverse laws and affairs of all states, commerce, regulation between states, militia arrangements, and some knowledge of foreign affairs (treaties, commercial policy, law of nations). Some of this knowledge is best acquired by practical attention during service rather than solely by private study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical burdens and willingness to serve justify longer terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Longer terms reduce the burdens (e.g., travel, arrangements) that might deter fit men from serving if terms were only a single year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many representatives must travel long distances, extending the term to two years makes the office more practical and attractive to capable individuals. Re-election expectations differ between delegates to the old Congress and representatives elected directly by the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and incentives around disputed/spurious elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual terms can encourage unlawful means of obtaining returns because disputed elections cannot be investigated and remedied in time; longer terms reduce that incentive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each house judges elections and qualifications; with only a year in office, a wrongly seated member might retain seat long enough to achieve his purpose before investigation disposes of him. Biennial terms make such fraud less rewarding and therefore less likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment standard: population as primary measure
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of people in each State ought to be the standard for regulating the proportion of those who are to represent the people of each State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation by population is the natural and universal connection for personal rights. While imperfect as a measure of wealth (taxation), it is the least objectionable practicable rule and had general sanction among the States; the same federal rule will be applied to direct taxes as to representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting slaves in apportionment (three-fifths compromise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slaves are to be regarded in a mixed character — in some respects persons, in others property — and the Constitution compromises by regarding the slave as 'divested of two fifths of the man' (i.e., counting three-fifths).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison's defense: state laws treat slaves partly as persons (protected and punishable) and partly as property (vendible, compelled labor). The compromise avoids inconsistency between representation and taxation and recognizes practical state policies toward suffrage; it is presented as a mutual moderation acceptable to both sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation should take account of property/wealth interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Government protects both persons and property; therefore some attention should be paid to property in choosing the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individuals' wealth often influences votes indirectly within a state, but states do not influence other states through personal influence; to secure the de facto weight of wealth and interest among states, representation ought to reflect comparative wealth where justifiable. This is used to justify giving larger or richer states greater representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use same census for representation and taxation to counteract bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Extending the same rule (aggregate inhabitants) to both apportionment of representation and of direct taxes produces opposite incentives and will control and balance state bias toward inflating or shrinking counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If representation alone were tied to the census, states would over-report inhabitants; if taxation alone, they'd under-report. Using the same rule for both produces internal checks on manipulation and encourages greater impartiality and co-operation in obtaining accurate censuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate total number and scaling of representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislature needs a certain minimum number to secure effective consultation and guard against improper combinations, but must be kept within limits to avoid confusion and mob passion; numbers should increase over time by constitutional limits (e.g., one representative per 30,000 after first census).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison notes wide disparity among state legislatures and warns against arithmetic extrapolation (e.g., Rhode Island ratios inappropriate for Virginia). The proposed plan—starting at 65, with census-driven increases—balances immediate practicability with long-term growth (projected increases to 100, 200, 400 over decades). The ideal is pragmatic: enough members for deliberation but not so many as to produce disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaller federal assembly acceptable because of institutional checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the federal legislature's powers are limited and it will be subject to observation and counteraction by state legislatures, a smaller number of representatives is an acceptable and safe temporary arrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion underlies acceptance of an initially small House (65 members): state legislatures will watch and counteract federal incursions; the limited scope of federal powers reduces temptation and capacity for abuse; and the public's temper and political character make the risk of conspiratorial tyranny among a small number improbable in the near term.
